newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives keep election focus on tax.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives keep election focus on tax.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives, trailing far behind Labour ahead of a May 1 election, went on the offensive on Friday against what they said were profligate spending plans by the main opposition party.
Prime Minister John Major told a news conference that a one penny cut in income tax, which will boost British pay packets from next week, would quickly be reversed if Labour wins power.

"At one stroke, this weekend's tax cut could be wiped out in July," Major told a news conference at which the Conservatives unveiled their latest slogan -- "Tory tax cuts in April, Labour tax rises in July."

The standard rate of income tax drops to 23 percent as of Sunday following finance minister Kenneth Clarke's November budget. In their manifesto on Wednesday, the Conservatives declared their aim of a 20 percent rate.
Major said Labour had committed itself to a budget within weeks of an election victory because it knew taxes would have to rise to pay for its pledges.
"I want people to know, while we are two days away from Conservative tax cuts, we could be just weeks away from the first Labour tax rise," he said.
The Conservatives are desperately trying to repeat their 1992 election success when attacks on Labour's tax policy scared voters away from the opposition party at the last minute.
But with two new opinion polls giving Labour leads of 21 and 24 points over the Conservatives, and with Labour promising it will not touch income tax rates, the task in 1997 is enormous.
Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, said Labour's plans would leave a 12 billion pounds ($19.69 billion) spending "black hole" over the next two years.

Under a Labour government, he claimed local councils would be freed to spend an extra 2.5 billion pounds a year, a halt to the privatisation programme would rob government coffers of 1.5 billion and plans to tackle unemployment and cut tax on heating fuel would also be costly.
"In his emergency budget, (Labour economics spokesman) Gordon Brown is going to have to put taxes up or increase borrowing," he told the news conference.

Brown hit back, demanding to know how Conservative plans to cut tax for married people who choose to stay at home to care for children or disabled relatives, at a cost of 1.2 billion stg, would be paid for.
"The Tories are in disarray on the public finances," Brown said. "Where is the money coming from to pay for their 15 billion pounds of tax and spending commitments?"

Brown and Labour leader Tony Blair have tried to remove Labour's reputation among voters as a party dedicated to spending heavily on social programmes and taxing Britons heavily to pay for the schemes.

Launching his party's manifesto, Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, accused both Labour and the Conservatives of running away from the need for higher taxes to improve Britain's basic public services.

Pledging to raise income tax by one point to pay for improvements in education and to increase tax on cigarettes to improve health care, Ashown declared: "Though the challenges are immense, the solutions we are offered are all too often puny." ($1=.6094 Stg)
